doc.title: Jimmy Heath — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Tenure at Queens College and building jazz studies
summary: Heath recalls his Queens College years, the endowed chair, colleagues he brought in, and his student Antonio Hart.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: That’s wonderful. Well you made reference to some of your students. Perhaps we should talk about education and your involvement in music education, first. Since the original Smithsonian Oral History on you, which took place in 1995, you have left your position at Queens College. You had an eleven-year tenure, is that correct?
That’s correct, I went there, I think in ’86, not ’85. I left in ’90…
’97, ’98. Bill did my…up at the Lincon Center, “Cosby King.” He was the emcee for my retirement.
Was that to endow a chair?
Yeah, that was happened. They endowed a chair in my name at Queens College, the Aaron Copland School of Music, that is.
And were you director of jazz studies? What was your position?

Yeah, I was basically that. I had…I was probably the first one that was put on a tenure track. Frank Foster and Bud Johnson, the tenor saxophonist from Earl Hines days who was great composer and saxophonist, was there as an adjunct before I got there. But, I was the first one hired full time at the Aaron Copland School of Music. After I was appointed I think I got Dr. Donald Byrd over there, and Sir Roland Hanna. Since that time, I was instrumental in getting Michael Mossman; he’s the head of the program now. My student is the saxophone teacher, and that’s Antonio Hart.
Yes, if a student is a reflection of his teacher, you’ve had some very good students.

Yes, he’s a wonderful young man, very respectful. I can’t get him to call me Jimmy, it’s always Mr. Heath. We hang out, play with the Dizzy band, do recordings together, and everything, “Mr. Heath, Mr. Heath,” but that’s him. So I wrote a piece for him called, “Like A Son” That’s putting it kind of exaggerated, because my kids don’t call me Mr. Heath.
What you wish a son would be like, right?
